procedures.title: Superheat Method (Fixed Orifice / Piston Systems)
procedures.purpose: Verify refrigerant charge on systems with fixed metering device
steps: System must run at least 15 minutes before taking readings
Outdoor ambient must be above 65°F for accurate readings
Measure suction pressure at service valve
Convert suction pressure to saturation temperature using PT chart
Measure actual suction line temperature 6 inches from compressor
Superheat = Actual suction line temp − Suction saturation temp
Use manufacturer's charging chart if available (based on indoor wet bulb + outdoor dry bulb)
Generic targets: 10-18°F superheat (varies with outdoor temp)
procedures.notes: This method ONLY works for fixed orifice/piston systems. For TXV systems, use the subcooling method.

procedures.title: Subcooling Method (TXV Systems)
procedures.purpose: Verify refrigerant charge on systems with TXV metering
steps: System must run at least 15 minutes
Measure discharge (high side) pressure
Convert discharge pressure to condensing temperature using PT chart
Measure actual liquid line temperature at condenser outlet (before filter drier)
Subcooling = Condensing saturation temp − Actual liquid line temp
Compare to manufacturer spec (typically on nameplate or service manual)
procedures.notes: TXV maintains constant superheat, so subcooling is the only reliable charge indicator for TXV systems.

procedures.title: Compressor Electrical Testing
procedures.purpose: Determine if compressor windings are healthy
steps: Disconnect all power and lock out
Discharge capacitor
Remove wires from compressor terminals (C, S, R)
Set ohmmeter to lowest range
Measure C to R: should be lowest resistance (run winding)
Measure C to S: should be higher resistance (start winding)
Measure R to S: should equal C-R + C-S (within 3%)
Measure each terminal to compressor shell/ground: must be infinity (OL)
Any reading to ground = grounded compressor = replace
If all readings are OL (open): open winding = replace
Single-phase scroll compressors: also check for reverse rotation
procedures.notes: ALWAYS test capacitor and voltage BEFORE condemning compressor. A bad capacitor is the #1 misdiagnosis for a bad compressor.

procedures.title: Airflow Verification
procedures.purpose: Verify proper indoor airflow for correct system operation
steps: Standard airflow: 400 CFM per ton of cooling (±10%)
Measure temperature split: return air temp minus supply air temp
Normal cooling delta-T: 16-22°F across evaporator
High delta-T (>24°F) = low airflow (check filter, blower, ducts)
Low delta-T (<14°F) = too much airflow or low charge
Check static pressure: total external should not exceed equipment rating
Typical: 0.5" WC total external static pressure for residential
Filter pressure drop should be < 0.3" WC for 1" filter
If possible, measure airflow at supply registers and sum

lowStaticPressure: Return air leak at air handler

procedures.title: Electrical Supply Verification
procedures.purpose: Verify proper voltage supply to equipment
steps: Check voltage at disconnect: L1-L2 should be within ±10% of nameplate
240V system: acceptable range 216V-264V
208V system: acceptable range 187V-229V
Check voltage under load (compressor running) - should not drop more than 3%
Check leg balance: L1-to-neutral vs L2-to-neutral should be within 2V
For 3-phase: measure all three legs, imbalance >2% can damage compressor
Check amp draw on each leg - should be balanced
Verify wire gauge adequate for amp draw and distance from panel
commonIssues: Loose wire connections causing voltage drop under load
Single-phasing on 3-phase equipment (loss of one leg)

procedures.title: Refrigerant Leak Detection
steps: Check service valve caps and Schrader cores first (most common leak points)
Use electronic leak detector - sweep all brazed joints slowly
Check flare connections at indoor coil and line set
Inspect evap coil - look for oil stains indicating leak
Check condenser coil - especially bottom rows
Look for oil stains at any connection point
If leak not found: nitrogen pressure test to 150 psig, monitor for 24 hours
Stubborn leaks: add UV dye, run system, return with UV light
Check condensate drain pan - refrigerant oil can accumulate there from evap leak
commonLeakLocations: Schrader valve cores (vibration loosens over time) - 25%

procedures.title: Furnace Sequence of Operation Diagnostic
procedures.purpose: Systematically diagnose any no-heat or intermittent-heat furnace fault by following the heating sequence and identifying which stage fails
steps: Read IFC board flash code FIRST — most boards flash a fault code that directly identifies which stage failed
STAGE 0 - Power and call: Verify 120V at furnace, 24VAC between R and C on board, then 24VAC at W when thermostat calls. No 24V = transformer, control board, or thermostat issue.

STAGE 1 - Inducer start: When W energized, IFC should energize inducer immediately. No inducer = check IFC inducer relay, inducer winding (typically 5-20 ohms), capacitor on PSC inducers, line voltage to inducer.

STAGE 2 - Pressure switch close: Inducer creates negative pressure; pressure switch contacts close within 10-20 seconds. Test by jumping PS terminals (diagnostic only, never permanent). If jumping makes it work: blocked vent, full condensate trap, collapsed hose, weak inducer, or bad switch. Measure inducer suction with manometer (-0.4 to -1.5 inches WC typical).

STAGE 3 - Ignitor warmup: Pressure switch proven, IFC sends 120V to HSI for 15-45 seconds. Visual: HSI should glow bright orange/white. Ohm test cold HSI: 50-200 ohms typical silicon nitride. Open circuit = replace. Visible cracks = replace.

STAGE 4 - Gas valve open: After HSI warmup, IFC sends 24VAC to gas valve MV terminal. Listen/feel for click. Verify 24VAC at valve terminals while energized. Manifold pressure should rise to 3.5 inches WC NG (10-11 inches WC LP). No gas at burners = bad valve coil (ohm test 30-80 ohms), wiring, or upstream gas supply issue.

STAGE 5 - Ignition: Burners should ignite from HSI within 1-3 seconds of gas valve opening. Watch flame pattern through inspection port — should be blue with light yellow tips, engulfing flame sensor.

STAGE 6 - Flame proving: Flame sensor produces DC microamp signal via flame rectification. IFC must see signal within 4-7 second trial. Measure with DC microamp meter in series with sensor wire: 2-6 µA healthy, below 1 µA = clean sensor with fine emery cloth. If clean sensor still low: ground path issue, cracked porcelain, or weak flame.
STAGE 7 - Flame established: Once flame proven, IFC de-energizes HSI. If IFC keeps re-trying: flame signal dropping out intermittently.
STAGE 8 - Blower delay and start: After 30-90 second delay, blower energizes on heat speed. Verify blower runs at correct speed tap. ECM blowers ramp up over 30-60 sec.

STAGE 9 - Steady-state run: Monitor manifold pressure, temperature rise (within nameplate range), flame signal, all limits. Rise too high = airflow issue. Rise too low = overfired or low gas pressure.

STAGE 10 - Safety limits: High limit (160-200°F) opens on overheat. Rollout switches (manual reset, 300°F+) trip on flame escaping burner box — investigate thoroughly, never just reset without finding cause.
STAGE 11 - Cycle off: Thermostat satisfied, gas valve closes, inducer post-purges 15-30 sec, blower runs off-delay 60-180 sec

targetRanges.manifoldGasPressureNG: 3.5 inches WC single-stage, 1.7/3.5 inches WC two-stage
targetRanges.inletGasPressureNG: 5-10.5 inches WC static, minimum 5 inches WC under full load
targetRanges.pressureSwitchSetpoint: 0.4-1.5 inches WC vacuum (per label on switch)
targetRanges.coAirFreeFlue: Below 100 ppm air-free. Above 400 ppm = service required.
targetRanges.coSupplyAir: 0 ppm — any reading = cracked heat exchanger, shut down immediately

procedures.notes: Always read board flash code first — it tells you which stage failed. Document gas pressure, temp rise, flame signal, and combustion analysis on every furnace service. Never bypass safety switches.
commonMistakes: Bypassing pressure switch permanently — it protects against blocked vent and CO buildup
Replacing ignitor without checking why it failed (water from drain, voltage issues, vibration, handling with bare hands)
Cleaning flame sensor with sandpaper (leaves grit that re-coats sensor) — use fine emery cloth only
Resetting rollout switch without finding root cause — clogged heat exchanger, blocked flue, severe overfire
Skipping combustion analysis — CO levels are invisible without it

procedures.title: Heat Pump Defrost Diagnostic
procedures.purpose: Diagnose heat pump defrost system failures — frosted/iced outdoor coil, no defrost, or excessive defrost cycling in heating mode
steps: Verify ice condition: light frost is normal in heating mode. Heavy ice over 50% of coil area or solid sheet of ice = defrost failure.
Check defrost initiation conditions: outdoor coil temp must be at or below 30°F AND time between defrosts has elapsed (30/60/90 min selectable on most boards) AND compressor must be running.
Locate defrost board in outdoor unit control box — identify timer selection jumper (T1/T2) and forced defrost test pads.
Force a defrost: short the test pins on the board with a small jumper (board manufacturer-specific). System should enter defrost within seconds if board is functioning.

Defrost sequence verification: (1) reversing valve energizes and shifts to cooling mode, (2) outdoor fan STOPS, (3) compressor continues running, (4) auxiliary heat strips energize at indoor unit (prevents cold draft indoors).
Defrost termination: ends when defrost thermostat opens (coil reaches ~60-80°F) OR 10-minute time-out, whichever comes first.
Test defrost thermostat: clip-on bimetal type — should be closed (continuity) below 32°F, open above ~60-80°F. Test with ohmmeter at ambient temperature.
Test reversing valve solenoid coil: ohm test 7-15 ohms typical (24VAC coil). Listen/feel for click when solenoid energizes and de-energizes.
Test reversing valve slide: with system in heat, discharge line to indoor coil should be very hot (180-220°F). When defrost initiates, that line goes cool and outdoor discharge line becomes hot.
If reversing valve solenoid clicks but valve does not shift: stuck slider valve. Tap firmly with rubber mallet during mode change while unit running. If still stuck: replace valve.
Verify outdoor fan STOPS during defrost — if fan runs continuously, defrost is ineffective (cold air keeps coil frozen).
Verify auxiliary heat (W2) energizes during defrost — prevents cold air complaints from occupants.

targetRanges.defrostInterval: 30, 60, or 90 minutes between defrosts (jumper-selectable on control board)
targetRanges.defrostDuration: 2-10 minutes typical (terminates on coil temperature or time limit)
targetRanges.outdoorCoilTempInHeat: Should be 10-25°F below outdoor ambient when running in heat mode

procedures.notes: Demand defrost boards (newer units) use both temperature sensors and pressure differential or runtime to decide when to defrost — more efficient than time/temp boards. Mini-splits handle defrost via main control board with no separate defrost board — check error codes on indoor display.
commonMistakes: Replacing defrost board when defrost sensor was actually failed — sensor is much cheaper
Wrong jumper settings on universal replacement board — causes too-frequent or no defrosts
Misreading normal thin frost as defrost board failure — uniform frost is expected in heat mode
Forgetting to verify outdoor fan stops during defrost — common board relay failure
Not checking that auxiliary heat energizes during defrost — cold draft complaint is often W2 not engaging

procedures.title: Total External Static Pressure Measurement
procedures.purpose: Measure total external static pressure (TESP) to diagnose airflow problems, blower stress, and duct system issues
steps: Tools required: digital manometer, drill with 3/16 or 1/4 inch bit, static pressure tip probes, foam plugs to seal test holes.
Run blower at full cooling speed (or heating speed for furnace tests) for at least 5 minutes to stabilize before reading.

Reading 1 - SUPPLY: Drill test port in supply plenum AFTER the cooling coil and AFTER any heat strip section, before first branch takeoff. Insert static probe pointing upstream. Record positive pressure (e.g., +0.32 inches WC).
Reading 2 - RETURN: Drill test port in return plenum BEFORE the filter, before the coil. Insert probe pointing downstream (toward blower). Record negative pressure (e.g., -0.18 inches WC).
Calculate TESP = absolute value of supply pressure + absolute value of return pressure. Example: 0.32 + 0.18 = 0.50 inches WC.
Compare to equipment nameplate: most residential rated 0.5 inches WC. Premium ECM equipment up to 0.8 inches WC. RTUs vary 1.0-2.0 inches WC.
Reading 3 - FILTER DROP: Measure pressure drop across filter only. Should be less than 0.10 inches WC new 1-inch pleated filter. Above 0.20 inches WC = replace filter.
Reading 4 - COIL DROP: Measure pressure drop across evaporator coil only. Clean dry coil: 0.10-0.25 inches WC. Wet coil: 0.20-0.35 inches WC. Above 0.40 inches WC = dirty coil.
Plug all drilled test holes with foam plugs or self-adhesive foam tape.
If TESP exceeds nameplate: investigate root causes (dirty filter, undersized ducts, closed registers, dirty coil, collapsed flex duct).

targetRanges.residentialTESP: 0.5 inches WC nominal, do not exceed nameplate (typically 0.5-0.8 inches WC)
targetRanges.filterDropNew1inch: Less than 0.10 inches WC for new 1-inch pleated filter
targetRanges.filterDropReplace: Replace when drop exceeds 0.20 inches WC across same filter

procedures.notes: Always note blower speed setting — many residential systems shipped on lowest tap. ECM blowers compensate for static by increasing power — high static can hide itself in CFM but shows up as elevated motor amp draw and noise. Record all readings for service history comparison.
commonMistakes: Not running blower long enough before reading — airflow not fully stabilized
Drilling test port in wrong location (before coil on supply side, or after filter on return side) — gives incorrect TESP
Probing perpendicular to airflow instead of parallel — velocity pressure adds error to static reading
Forgetting to plug test holes after measurement — permanent air leak in duct system
Comparing to generic 0.5 inches WC rule without checking actual nameplate rating
Missing that high static plus low amp draw means airflow blocked downstream of the measurement point

procedures.title: Mini-Split Commissioning & Error Code Diagnostic
procedures.purpose: Properly commission a new mini-split installation and diagnose error codes from indoor unit display
steps: PRE-STARTUP CHECKLIST:
1. Verify line set length within manufacturer spec (typical 25 ft pre-charged, max 50-100 ft depending on brand with added refrigerant per ft)
2. Verify height differential within spec (typical max indoor above outdoor 24-49 ft, outdoor above indoor 24 ft — brand-specific)
3. Inspect flares: 45 degree angle, smooth, no cracks, proper torque per OEM torque table
4. Confirm line set insulation continuous, no compression, vapor barrier sealed
5. Verify drain line slope minimum 1/4 inch per foot, terminated appropriately
6. Confirm communication wire correct gauge (typically 14 AWG stranded shielded), polarity verified (most brands polarity-sensitive)
7. Confirm disconnect within sight of outdoor unit, properly sized breaker per nameplate MOCP
STARTUP PROCEDURE:
1. Pressure test line set and indoor coil with dry nitrogen to manufacturer spec (typically 550 psig for R-410A) for minimum 60 minutes — watch for any pressure drop
2. Evacuate line set and indoor coil to 500 microns or lower — measure with micron gauge at far end of line set, not at pump
3. Standing vacuum test: isolate from pump, vacuum must hold below 1000 microns for 15 minutes minimum
4. Open service valves at outdoor unit — first liquid (small valve), then suction (large valve) — using correct hex key, fully counter-clockwise to backseat
5. Add additional refrigerant if line set exceeds pre-charged length (per OEM g/m or oz/ft specification)
6. Apply power — allow standby time per manual (typically 12 hours crankcase heater warmup on initial startup; 1 hour minimum)
7. Start in cooling mode, let inverter ramp up over 2-5 minutes
8. Verify: outdoor fan running, indoor fan running, supply temp dropping in cooling, compressor amp draw within range
9. Run minimum 30 minutes then verify pressures, temperatures, and document all readings
ERROR CODE DIAGNOSTIC:
1. Note exact code displayed — format varies by brand
2. Power-cycle once to clear soft faults (some codes are latching, others self-clear)
3. Consult brand-specific code chart — codes are very specific, do not guess

4. Common code categories: communication (wiring/polarity), sensor (thermistor open/short), refrigerant (low pressure/high pressure/discharge temp), compressor (overcurrent/position error), EEV (stepper feedback)
5. Use manufacturer service tool or app if available — reveals live operating data, sensor values, compressor frequency

Mitsubishi.U2: High discharge temperature or refrigerant shortage

LG.CH05: Communication error between indoor and outdoor
LG.CH07: Indoor unit mode mismatch on multi-zone system

targetRanges.vacuumLevel: 500 microns or lower before opening service valves (300 microns preferred)
targetRanges.standingVacuumTest: Holds below 1000 microns for 15 min after pump isolation
targetRanges.nitrogenPressureTest: 550 psig for R-410A for minimum 60 minutes

commonMistakes: Skipping nitrogen pressure test — missed flare leak causes charge loss within days
Cracking open service valve before evacuating — moisture and air contaminate system permanently
Reversed communication wire polarity — most brands refuse to operate, throws communication error
Using vacuum pump gauge to verify micron level instead of proper micron gauge — wildly inaccurate
Not allowing crankcase heater warmup before first start in cold ambient — flooded compressor startup failure
Replacing parts based on guessing — mini-split error codes are precise, always look up the specific code

procedures.title: Condenser and Evaporator Coil Cleaning Procedure
procedures.purpose: Properly clean fouled coils to restore heat transfer without damaging fins, copper, or aluminum
steps: Pre-cleaning assessment: visually inspect coil for fin density (FPI), existing damage, and foulant type (cottonwood, dust, grass clippings, grease, biological growth). Choose chemical accordingly.
Disconnect and lock out power at disconnect before any wet cleaning.
Cover all electrical components, motors, contactors, and control boards with plastic to prevent water and chemical intrusion.
CONDENSER (outdoor) coil cleaning:
1. Remove top grille and fan assembly to gain access for inside-out cleaning.
2. Pre-rinse with garden hose at normal household pressure — NEVER use pressure washer (bends fins, damages protective coating, drives debris deeper into coil).
3. Apply alkaline cleaner (pH 9-12) such as Nu-Calgon CalClean for normal dirt and grease — foaming type recommended.
4. Allow dwell time per product label (5-10 min typical) — do not let cleaner dry on coil.
5. Rinse from INSIDE-OUT through the coil with garden hose, top to bottom, until water runs completely clear.
6. NEVER use acid cleaner on outdoor coil — will pit aluminum and corrode copper-to-aluminum connections.
EVAPORATOR (indoor) coil cleaning:
1. Access via coil access panel — remove screws, may need to cut and reseal duct mastic.
2. For light biofilm: use no-rinse evaporator coil cleaner (foaming alkaline, self-rinsing via condensate drain) — apply, let soak, condensate drain washes residue out.
3. For heavy fouling: alkaline cleaner with garden hose rinse (same as condenser procedure).
4. NEVER use acid cleaner on evaporator coil — attacks aluminum fins and copper tubes.
5. Flush drain pan and drain line after coil cleaning — vacuum trap, flush with vinegar/water mix.
MICROCHANNEL coil special instructions:
1. Microchannel (MCHX) coils are aluminum throughout — alkaline cleaner only, never acid cleaner.
2. Garden hose pressure only — fins damage more easily than traditional fin-and-tube.
3. Do not use fin combs on MCHX — flat aluminum channels cannot be combed.
FIN STRAIGHTENING (traditional fin-and-tube only):
1. Use fin comb sized to coil FPI (count fins per inch first — residential typically 10-15 FPI).
2. Comb gently in direction of fin orientation, never across fins.
3. More than 30% fin damage: replacement is more cost-effective than cleaning.

targetRanges.rinseWaterPressure: Garden hose only, approximately 40-60 psi — never pressure washer
targetRanges.cleanerPHAlkaline: pH 9-12 (safe for aluminum fins and copper tubes)
targetRanges.cleanerPHAcid: pH 1-3 (ONLY for specific copper fin-and-tube outdoor coils with manufacturer approval — NEVER on aluminum MCHX)
targetRanges.deltaTImprovementAfterClean: Temperature split should improve 3-5°F after thorough coil cleaning

procedures.notes: Document before and after temperatures and pressures to demonstrate service value. Microchannel coils are increasingly common on outdoor units — always identify coil type before selecting cleaning method.
commonMistakes: Using pressure washer — permanently bends fins, voids warranty, drives debris deeper
Using acid cleaner on aluminum microchannel coil — destroys coil within months
Spraying cleaner from outside-in instead of inside-out on condenser — pushes debris into coil core
Not covering electrical components before wet cleaning — moisture damages contactors and PCBs
Letting cleaner dry on coil — leaves stains and residue that continue corroding
Not addressing why coil was dirty (vegetation too close, no protective screen, dryer vent nearby)

procedures.title: System Evacuation and Vacuum Verification
procedures.purpose: Properly evacuate refrigerant system to remove non-condensables and moisture, then verify with micron gauge before charging
steps: Tools required: 6 CFM minimum two-stage vacuum pump (8 CFM preferred for 3+ ton), large-bore vacuum-rated hoses (1/2 or 3/8 inch ID — NOT standard 1/4 inch charging hoses), digital micron gauge (thermistor-based), Schrader core removal tools, fresh vacuum pump oil.
Pre-evacuation: confirm leak is repaired (nitrogen pressure test held). Replace filter drier — new drier is critical for moisture control.
Remove BOTH Schrader cores using core remover tool — cores create major restriction, evacuating through them takes 5x longer.
Connect pump and micron gauge to OPPOSITE ends of system if possible — micron gauge on indoor service port, pump on outdoor. NEVER measure microns at pump — reads false low.
Verify vacuum pump oil is clean and full. Open ballast valve initially (1-5 minutes) to purge moisture from oil, then close.
Pull vacuum to 500 microns minimum (300 microns preferred, especially for R-410A POE systems).
TRIPLE EVACUATION METHOD (best practice for moisture-contaminated systems):
1st pull: vacuum to 1500 microns, isolate pump, break vacuum with dry nitrogen to 2-5 psig
2nd pull: vacuum to 1000 microns, isolate, break with dry nitrogen to 2-5 psig
3rd pull: vacuum to 500 microns or below
DECAY TEST (standing vacuum hold test):
1. Pull system to 500 microns or lower
2. Isolate pump from system (close valve between pump and manifold — do NOT shut off pump)
3. Watch micron gauge for 15-30 minutes
INTERPRETATION:
Holds below 1000 microns = system dry, no leak, ready to charge
Rises slowly past 2000 microns and keeps climbing = moisture still boiling off (re-evacuate longer)
Rises rapidly past 5000 microns or returns toward atmospheric = leak (find and repair before charging)
Stabilizes at 2000-4000 microns = marginal moisture, acceptable on some systems, re-evacuate for R-410A or VRF
Reinstall Schrader cores (with new gaskets) after decay test passes.
System ready for refrigerant charge.

targetRanges.minimumVacuumR410A: 500 microns (300 microns preferred for POE systems)
targetRanges.decayTestPass: Holds below 1000 microns for 15 minutes after pump isolation
targetRanges.atmosphericPressure: 760,000 microns (760 mmHg) — we evacuate to 1500x lower
targetRanges.waterBoilingPoint: Water boils at 75°F at approximately 22,500 microns — below this threshold water actively evaporates out of system during evacuation

procedures.notes: Large-bore hoses make a 5-10x difference in evacuation time compared to 1/4-inch charging hoses. Change vacuum pump oil after every heavy moisture evacuation — contaminated oil cannot achieve deep vacuum. A slow decay (moisture) looks very different from a fast decay (leak) — learn to distinguish them.
commonMistakes: Reading microns at pump rather than far end of system — drastically underestimates actual system vacuum level
Using 1/4-inch charging hoses for evacuation — massive restriction extends time by 5-10x
Leaving Schrader cores in during evacuation — reduces conductance by approximately 80%
Stopping at 2000 microns when it stops dropping — usually means moisture is boiling off, need more time or triple-evac
Not running decay test — confirms vacuum but does not verify seal integrity against leaks
Forgetting to change vacuum pump oil — contaminated oil cannot achieve 300-500 micron vacuum
Charging at 5000 microns as good enough — leads to acid formation, copper plating, and compressor failure within 1-3 years
Not replacing filter drier with every refrigerant circuit opening — drier holds moisture you thought you evacuated
